title: Scientists Reveal Earth Has Six Continents, Not Seven—New Study Shakes Geography Norms
body:
A new geophysical study is turning the long‑standing seven‑continent model on its head, arguing that the Earth may actually consist of only six continents. The research, published this week, suggests that Europe and North America are not fully separated by the Atlantic Ocean but remain linked by a deep‑sea ridge that could be considered a continuous landmass beneath the water. If the findings gain wider acceptance, textbooks, school curricula and even global geopolitics could be forced to rethink a concept that has shaped human perception of the planet for centuries.

The team behind the study, led by Dr. Elena Martínez of the Institute for Tectonic Dynamics, used high‑resolution seismic tomography and mantle flow simulations to map the hidden structure of the Atlantic basin. Their data reveal a persistent, dense lithospheric bridge—dubbed the “Trans‑Atlantic Craton”—that stretches from the Iberian Peninsula across the Mid‑Atlantic Ridge to the eastern seaboard of North America. While the surface expression is the ocean, the underlying crust shares similar composition, age and thermal characteristics with the adjoining continental plates, a trait more typical of contiguous continents than of fully independent ones.

Proponents of the traditional seven‑continent framework have long relied on cultural, historical and political criteria to delineate Europe from Asia and North America from South America. However, the new model emphasizes a purely geological definition: a continent is a large, contiguous expanse of continental crust that rests on the Earth's mantle. By that metric, the researchers argue that the Atlantic “gap” is superficial, and the underlying crustal continuity warrants treating Europe and North America as a single continental entity, which they term “Atlantica.” The authors acknowledge that the oceanic crust still separates the landmasses at the surface, but they point out that similar situations exist elsewhere—such as the submerged continent of Zealandia, which is already recognized despite being mostly underwater.

The study has sparked vigorous debate among geologists, educators and policymakers. Critics caution that redefining continents on the basis of deep‑earth structures could create confusion, especially given the entrenched cultural identities tied to the current model. “Continents are not just geological units; they are also social constructs,” said Professor James O’Leary, a cultural geographer at the University of Toronto. “Changing the map could have ripple effects on everything from sports competitions to international agreements that reference continental boundaries.” Others, however, welcome the fresh perspective, noting that scientific classifications have evolved before—consider the reclassification of Pluto or the acceptance of plate tectonics itself.

Beyond academic discourse, the findings could have practical implications for resource exploration and environmental policy. A unified Atlantica might influence how nations approach trans‑Atlantic marine protected areas, deep‑sea mining rights, and climate‑change mitigation strategies that consider oceanic and continental interactions as a single system. Moreover, the research underscores the importance of advanced imaging technologies that can peer through kilometers of water and rock, potentially unveiling other hidden connections beneath the planet’s surface.

As the scientific community digests the evidence, the conversation about what truly defines a continent is poised to expand beyond textbooks. Whether the six‑continent model will replace the familiar seven‑continent schema remains uncertain, but the study serves as a reminder that even the most basic elements of our worldview are subject to revision. Future research, especially collaborative international surveys of the Atlantic crust, will determine if the proposed Atlantica will be embraced or relegated to a provocative footnote in the ongoing quest to understand Earth’s dynamic interior.
